docs.title: What is paulrun?
docs.text:
paulrun runs hand-written markdown runbooks.

A runbook is a normal markdown file that a person can read and follow without paulrun. Mark a code block run, and paulrun runs it for you. Everything else stays documentation.

docs.title: Example runbook
docs.text:
---
title: Release my-package
output_path: logs/release-<VERSION>.md
inputs:
  - name: VERSION
    description: The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0
    pattern: '^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$'
---

# Releasing my-package

## Run the tests

```sh run
make test
```

## Tag the release

```sh run
git tag <VERSION>
git push origin <VERSION>
```

## Publish on GitHub

```confirm
Create a GitHub release from tag <VERSION>.
```

Check it, then run it:

paulrun check RELEASING.md
paulrun go RELEASING.md

paulrun asks for the version, shows you the plan, and runs each step in order, streaming every command's output as it goes. It stops at the first command that fails, and waits for you at the GitHub step, since that one is done by hand:

VERSION (The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0): 1.2.0
Release my-package
inputs: VERSION=1.2.0
  1. Run the tests
  2. Tag the release
  3. Publish on GitHub
2 run blocks
Start? [y/N] y

=== Run the tests ===
    make test
...
exit 0 (4.2s)

=== Tag the release ===
    git tag 1.2.0
    git push origin 1.2.0
...
exit 0 (1.3s)

=== Publish on GitHub ===
Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0.
Continue? [y/N] y

finished: ok (12.8s)
transcript: logs/release-1.2.0.md

Every run is also recorded in logs/release-1.2.0.md, so you can see afterwards exactly what ran and what it printed.

docs.title: Why use paulrun?
docs.text:
Release steps get forgotten. Writing them down helps; making the written-down version run itself fixes it.

  • It's just markdown - A runbook reads like documentation, renders on GitHub, and works fine without paulrun.
  • Check before you run - paulrun check catches undeclared placeholders, broken frontmatter and shell or Python syntax errors before anything runs.
  • See what would happen - paulrun go --dry shows every command with its inputs filled in, and runs nothing.
  • Inputs and secrets - Ask for values once, check them against a pattern, and keep secrets out of the screen and the log.
  • Manual steps too - confirm blocks pause for the things only a person can do.
  • A record of every run - An optional transcript keeps every command, its output and how the run finished.
  • More than shell - Shell and Python blocks are built in, and other languages can be added as backends.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Install paulrun
  • The runbook format: everything a runbook can contain
  • The command line: every command, flag and exit code
  • Backends: the languages paulrun runs, and adding your own

Initial release. paulrun runs hand-written markdown runbooks.

  • paulrun go runs a runbook's steps in order, streaming each block's output as it's printed and stopping at the first block that fails.
  • run blocks for shell (sh, bash, shell) and Python (python, py), with the python frontmatter key to choose the interpreter.
  • docstring blocks to show notes as the runbook runs, and confirm blocks to pause for steps done by hand.
  • input blocks to ask for a value part way through a run, once it exists: a pull request number from a step done by hand, or a one-time code that expires in seconds.
  • Inputs, collected from the environment or by asking, with an optional pattern to check them against. Plain inputs fill in <NAME> placeholders; secrets are hidden as you type them and replaced with **** everywhere paulrun shows or records them.
  • paulrun go --dry to see every block with its inputs filled in, without running anything.
  • paulrun go --step to run, skip or quit at each block.
  • Transcripts: with output_path set, every run is added to a plain record of what ran, what it printed and how it finished.
  • Ctrl-C stops a run cleanly, letting a running block stop and recording how far the run got.
  • paulrun check to find problems before running anything: missing or malformed frontmatter, undeclared placeholders, secrets used as placeholders, blocks outside a step, and shell and Python syntax errors, with shellcheck warnings when it's installed.
  • paulrun inputs to list the inputs a runbook needs, and paulrun backends to list the languages paulrun can run.
  • Backends for other languages can be added by any package, through the paulrun.backends entry point group.

docs.title: 🔌 Backends
docs.text:
A backend runs run blocks for one or more languages. paulrun comes with two, for shell and Python, and other languages can be added by any package.

Run paulrun backends to see which backends are installed, the languages each one runs, and the package it comes from:

python  python, py       paulrun.backends.python:PythonBackend (paulrun 0.1.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  paulrun.backends.shell:ShellBackend (paulrun 0.1.0)

docs.title: shell
docs.text:
Languages: sh, bash, shell. Needs bash.

Each block runs as one bash script that stops at the first command that fails, as if it began with set -eo pipefail. check finds syntax errors with bash -n, and adds shellcheck warnings if it's installed. See Shell blocks.

docs.title: python
docs.text:
Languages: python, py. Needs nothing extra.

Each block runs as its own script, with the command in the runbook's python frontmatter key, or with the Python paulrun runs on. check finds syntax errors by compiling each block. See Python blocks.

docs.title: Writing a backend
docs.text:
A backend is a plain class with a name, the languages it runs, and two methods: validate() checks a block without running it, and run() runs it. It doesn't need a base class; it only has to look like this protocol, from paulrun.backends:

class Backend(Protocol):
    """Runs `run` blocks for one or more languages.

    Backends are classes registered under the `paulrun.backends` entry point group. Each is created
    once, with no arguments, when backends are loaded.
    """

    # Read-only, so a backend can set them as plain class attributes.
    @property
    def name(self) -> str: ...

    @property
    def languages(self) -> tuple[str, ...]:
        """The fence languages this backend runs, e.g. ("sh", "bash")."""

    def validate(self, code: str) -> list[Problem]:
        """Return the problems found in a block, without running it. An empty list means it's fine.

        code is the block as written, so it can contain <NAME> placeholders. Replacing them with
        something this language accepts is up to the backend. Any error stops the runbook running;
        warnings are only reported.
        """

    def run(
        self,
        code: str,
        *,
        frontmatter: Mapping[str, Any],
        env: Mapping[str, str],
        cwd: Path,
        output: Callable[[str], None],
    ) -> int:
        """Run a block and return its exit code, where 0 means it succeeded.

        Call output with each line the block prints, without its newline, as soon as it's printed.
        Don't print anything directly; paulrun owns the terminal. frontmatter is the runbook's
        frontmatter, read-only. env is the block's complete environment and cwd is where it runs.
        """

Everything a backend needs is in paulrun.backends (Problem, stream and Interrupted) and paulrun.inputs (PLACEHOLDER).

docs.title: validate()
docs.text:
paulrun check calls validate() on every block in the backend's languages, and so does paulrun go, before anything runs. It returns a list of Problems:

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Problem:
    """Something a backend found wrong with a block."""

    message: str
    line: int | None = None  # line in the block, counting its first line as 1; None if it's about the whole block
    warning: bool = False  # warnings are reported but don't stop the runbook running
  • Lines count from the block's first line, as 1. paulrun turns them into lines in the runbook, so check points at the right place.
  • An error stops go before anything runs. A warning is shown, and the run carries on.

  • The code is as written, with <NAME> placeholders still in it. Before checking it, swap each one for something your language accepts. The built-in backends use the placeholder's bare name, which is a plain word in shell and a plain name in Python:

    from paulrun.inputs import PLACEHOLDER

script = PLACEHOLDER.sub(lambda match: match.group(1), code)

  • Check that what run() needs is installed. go always validates first, so an error here is far friendlier than run() failing to start.

docs.title: run()
docs.text:
run() gets:

  • code: the block with every placeholder replaced by its value. Secrets are never replaced; they're only in env.
  • frontmatter: the runbook's frontmatter, read-only, for a backend with settings of its own, like the Python backend's python key.
  • env: the block's complete environment, including every input. Pass it on as it is.
  • cwd: the folder the runbook is in, where the block runs.
  • output: call it with each line the block prints, as soon as it's printed.

It returns the block's exit code, where 0 means it succeeded and anything else stops the run.

A backend never prints. paulrun shows each line, replaces secrets with ****, and records it in the transcript, so a backend doesn't need to do any of that itself.

docs.title: stream()
docs.text:
Most backends run a command, and stream() does all of that for you:

def stream(command: Sequence[str], *, env: Mapping[str, str], cwd: Path, output: Callable[[str], None]) -> int:

It runs command, passes each line it prints to output as it's printed, and returns its exit code. It's what the built-in backends use, and it gets the details right:

  • stdout and stderr are merged, so lines are shown in the order they were printed.
  • The command shares paulrun's terminal, so it can still ask for a password the way git, ssh and gpg do.
  • Ctrl-C works. On the first press, the command gets the chance to stop by itself, and anything it prints on the way out is still shown. A second press kills it, and everything it started. Either way, once it's stopped, stream() raises Interrupted with its exit code, so the run can record how the block ended.

A backend that doesn't use stream() should do the same: once its block has stopped after Ctrl-C, raise Interrupted(exit_code). paulrun records the block's exit code, then finishes the run as interrupted.

docs.title: Shipping your own backend
docs.text:
Anyone can publish a backend in their own package. Once it's installed alongside paulrun, it loads exactly like a built-in one.

Here's a complete backend for Node.js, in a package called paulrun-node:

paulrun-node/
  pyproject.toml
  paulrun_node/
    __init__.py

paulrun_node/__init__.py:

import re
import shutil
import subprocess
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from paulrun.backends import Problem, stream
from paulrun.inputs import PLACEHOLDER


class NodeBackend:
    """Runs each block as a Node.js script."""

    name = "node"
    languages = ("js", "javascript")

    def validate(self, code: str) -> list[Problem]:
        if shutil.which("node") is None:
            return [Problem("node isn't installed")]
        # Swap each placeholder for its bare name, which is a plain identifier, so the code still parses.
        script = PLACEHOLDER.sub(lambda match: match.group(1), code)
        result = subprocess.run(["node", "--check"], input=script, capture_output=True, text=True)
        if result.returncode == 0:
            return []
        # node starts with where the error is, e.g. "[stdin]:3", and says what it is further down.
        where = re.match(r"\[stdin\]:(\d+)", result.stderr)
        errors = [line for line in result.stderr.splitlines() if line.startswith("SyntaxError: ")]
        return [Problem(errors[0] if errors else result.stderr.strip(), line=int(where.group(1)) if where else None)]

    def run(
        self,
        code: str,
        *,
        frontmatter: Mapping[str, Any],
        env: Mapping[str, str],
        cwd: Path,
        output: Callable[[str], None],
    ) -> int:
        return stream(["node", "-e", code], env=env, cwd=cwd, output=output)

pyproject.toml registers it under the paulrun.backends entry point group, which is how paulrun finds it:

[project]
name = "paulrun-node"
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["paulrun>=0.1.0"]

[project.entry-points."paulrun.backends"]
node = "paulrun_node:NodeBackend"

[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

Install it alongside paulrun:

uv tool install paulrun --with paulrun-node     # once it's on PyPI
uv tool install paulrun --with ./paulrun-node   # from a local folder, while you work on it

With pip, install it into the same environment as paulrun. Then paulrun backends lists it:

node    js, javascript   paulrun_node:NodeBackend (paulrun-node 0.1.0)
python  python, py       paulrun.backends.python:PythonBackend (paulrun 0.1.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  paulrun.backends.shell:ShellBackend (paulrun 0.1.0)

and runbooks can use it:

---
title: Hello from Node
---

## Say hello

```js run
console.log(`Hello from Node ${process.version}`);
```

To test a backend, create it and call its methods directly, the way paulrun tests its own: call run() with output=lines.append and check the exit code and the lines, and call validate() on a broken block. See paulrun's backend tests.

docs.title: Things to know
docs.text:
• Each language can only have one backend. If two installed backends claim the same language, paulrun stops with an error naming both. paulrun backends shows which languages are taken.
  • Frontmatter keys of your own get a check warning. A backend can read its own settings from frontmatter, but check only knows paulrun's keys, so it warns about any other. The warning doesn't stop a run.

docs.title: Adding a backend to paulrun
docs.text:
A backend for a language lots of people use can ship with paulrun itself. Built-in backends load the same way as external ones, so it's the same code, in a different place:

  1. paulrun/backends/<name>.py, implementing the protocol. shell.py and python.py are good models: both use stream(), and swap placeholders before validating.

  2. One entry point line in paulrun's pyproject.toml, next to the built-in ones:

    [project.entry-points."paulrun.backends"]
shell = "paulrun.backends.shell:ShellBackend"
python = "paulrun.backends.python:PythonBackend"

    Then run make install, and uv run paulrun backends should list it.

  3. tests/backends/test_<name>.py, which really runs blocks in tmp_path, with no mocking. Skip the tests if the language isn't installed, e.g. pytest.mark.skipif(shutil.which("ruby") is None, reason="ruby isn't installed"). CI runs on GitHub's ubuntu-latest, which already has many languages; if yours isn't one of them, add a step to .github/workflows/ci.yml that installs it, so CI runs the tests rather than skipping them.

  4. A section on this page, under Built-in backends: its languages, what it needs installed, how it runs a block, and how check validates one.
  5. A CHANGELOG entry, in both CHANGELOG.md and docs/CHANGELOG.md.

CONTRIBUTING.md has the rest: setting up, and what to run before opening a pull request.

docs.title: 📟 Command line
docs.text:
paulrun go RUNBOOK [--dry] [--step]   # run a runbook
paulrun check RUNBOOK                 # find problems without running anything
paulrun inputs RUNBOOK                # list the inputs a runbook needs
paulrun backends                      # list the languages paulrun can run
paulrun --version

docs.title: paulrun go
docs.text:
Runs a runbook, step by step.

paulrun go RELEASING.md
  1. Checks the runbook first, exactly as paulrun check does. Any error stops it here, before anything runs. Warnings are shown, then it carries on.
  2. Collects the inputs, from the environment or by asking. See How inputs are collected.
  3. Shows the plan (the title, the inputs, each step, and how many blocks will run) and asks Start? [y/N].
  4. Goes through each step in order, showing its name, then each block: notes are shown, confirm blocks wait for y, input blocks ask for their value, and run blocks run with their output streamed as it's printed.
VERSION (The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0): 1.2.0
Release my-package
inputs: VERSION=1.2.0
  1. Run the tests
  2. Tag the release
  3. Publish on GitHub
2 run blocks
Start? [y/N] y

=== Run the tests ===
    make test
...
exit 0 (4.2s)

=== Tag the release ===
    git tag 1.2.0
...
exit 0 (0.1s)

=== Publish on GitHub ===
Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0.
Continue? [y/N] y

finished: ok (12.8s)
transcript: logs/release-1.2.0.md

The run stops at the first block that fails, and later steps don't run:

=== Build ===
    echo "Building"
    exit 2
Building
exit 2 (0.0s)

finished: failed at "Build" (exit 2)

Only y answers Start? and Continue? with a yes. Anything else, including just pressing enter, ends the run as aborted.

If the runbook has an output_path, the run is recorded there, and the last line says where.

docs.title: --dry
docs.text:
Shows what the runbook would do, without doing any of it.

paulrun go --dry RELEASING.md

Every block is shown with its inputs filled in, but nothing runs. There's no Start? question, confirm blocks don't wait, and no transcript is written. Frontmatter inputs are still collected, so the blocks can be filled in, but secrets aren't needed, so they aren't asked for and show as ****. input blocks aren't asked for either, since their values may not exist yet: each shows where the run would stop to ask, and later blocks show its placeholder as written.

VERSION (The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0): 1.2.0
Release my-package
inputs: VERSION=1.2.0
  1. Run the tests
  2. Tag the release
  3. Publish on GitHub
2 run blocks
dry run: nothing will be run

=== Run the tests ===
    make test

=== Tag the release ===
    git tag 1.2.0

=== Publish on GitHub ===
Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0.

finished: dry run, nothing was run

docs.title: --step
docs.text:
Asks about every run block before running it.

paulrun go --step RELEASING.md

After each block's code is shown, paulrun asks Run this block? [y]es / [s]kip / [q]uit:

  • y runs the block.
  • s skips it, and the run carries on with the next block.
  • q quits, and the run ends as aborted.

Any other answer gets the question again. Skipped blocks are marked as skipped in the transcript. --step only asks about run blocks; input blocks are always asked. With --dry, --step does nothing, since nothing runs anyway.

=== Build ===
    echo "Building"
Run this block? [y]es / [s]kip / [q]uit y
Building
exit 0 (0.0s)

=== Publish ===
    echo "Publishing"
Run this block? [y]es / [s]kip / [q]uit s
skipped (--step)

finished: ok (0.0s)

docs.title: Pressing Ctrl-C
docs.text:
Ctrl-C stops the run, cleanly:

  • If a block is running, it gets the Ctrl-C too, and paulrun waits for it to stop, still showing anything it prints. Its exit code is recorded.
  • If a block ignores Ctrl-C, press it again. paulrun stops the block and everything it started.
  • Later steps don't run, and the run ends as finished: interrupted at "<step>", in the transcript too.

docs.title: paulrun check
docs.text:
Finds problems in a runbook without running anything.

paulrun check RELEASING.md

RELEASING.md: ok

Each problem is shown with the line it's on, so your editor can jump to it, then a count:

broken.md:6: error: input VERSION is declared twice (first on line 4)
broken.md:8: warning: input BRANCH is never used
broken.md:12: error: run blocks must be inside a step (a ## heading)
broken.md:19: error: <TAG> isn't a declared input
broken.md:21: error: syntax error near unexpected token `fi'

4 errors, 1 warning

Errors are problems that would make the runbook go wrong:

  • a missing title, or a frontmatter value of the wrong type
  • an input without a name or description, a name that isn't UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, a name declared twice, or a pattern that isn't a valid regular expression
  • an input block that isn't valid YAML, or isn't a mapping
  • a placeholder that isn't a declared input, or a secret used as a placeholder
  • an input block's value used before the block, or in output_path
  • a run, docstring, confirm or input block before the first ## heading
  • a run block in a language no backend runs
  • a python command that isn't installed
  • a syntax error in a shell or Python block

Warnings are worth a look, but don't stop the runbook:

  • a frontmatter or input key paulrun doesn't know, which is often a typo
  • an input nothing uses
  • a Python SyntaxWarning, and shellcheck findings if it's installed

paulrun go runs the same checks before it starts.

docs.title: paulrun inputs
docs.text:
Lists the inputs a runbook needs, so you know what to have ready, or what to set in the environment.

paulrun inputs PUBLISHING.md

VERSION  The version being released, e.g. 1.2.0
         pattern: ^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$
PR       The number GitHub gave the pull request
         pattern: ^\d+$
         asked in "Open the pull request"
OTP      The code from your authenticator app
         pattern: ^\d{6}$
         secret
         asked in "Publish"

Frontmatter inputs come first. Inputs from input blocks come after, each with the step that asks for it.

If the rest of the runbook is broken, the frontmatter inputs are still listed; input blocks need the rest of the runbook to be readable. Inputs that are missing a name or description aren't listed; paulrun check reports those.

docs.title: paulrun backends
docs.text:
Lists the languages paulrun can run, and the package each one comes from.

paulrun backends

python  python, py       paulrun.backends.python:PythonBackend (paulrun 0.1.0)
shell   sh, bash, shell  paulrun.backends.shell:ShellBackend (paulrun 0.1.0)

Backends installed from other packages are listed here too.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Code Meaning 0 The run finished, or check found no errors. A --dry run, and a run where every block was skipped, exit 0 too. 1 A block failed, the run was aborted or interrupted, check found errors, or the runbook couldn't be read. 2 The command was used wrongly, e.g. a runbook that doesn't exist.

docs.title: 🚀 Install
docs.text: paulrun is a command-line tool, so install it on its own rather than into a project:

docs.title: uv
docs.text: uv tool install paulrun

docs.title: pip
docs.text:
pip install paulrun

Once installed, check it's working:

> paulrun --version
paulrun, version 0.1.0

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Python 3.12 or later.
  • macOS or Linux. Windows isn't supported.
  • bash, which runs shell blocks. It's on macOS and almost every Linux system already.

docs.title: Optional: shellcheck
docs.text:
If shellcheck is installed, paulrun check uses it to warn about common mistakes in shell blocks, such as an unquoted variable. Without it, shell blocks are still checked for syntax errors.

brew install shellcheck      # macOS
sudo apt install shellcheck  # Debian and Ubuntu

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• The runbook format to write your first runbook
  • The command line to see everything paulrun can do

docs.title: 📜 Runbook format
docs.text:
A runbook is a markdown file. Frontmatter at the top sets it up, each ## heading is a step, and fenced code blocks marked for paulrun are printed, paused on, or run. Everything else is documentation.

Run paulrun check on a runbook at any time to find out what's wrong with it.

docs.title: Frontmatter
docs.text:
YAML between --- lines at the very top of the file:

---
title: Release my-package                    # required
description: Release a new version.          # optional
output_path: logs/release-<VERSION>.md       # optional
python: uv run python                        # optional
inputs:                                      # optional
  - name: VERSION                            # required
    description: The version to release, e.g. 1.2.0   # required
    pattern: '^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$'               # optional
  - name: PUBLISH_TOKEN
    description: Token for the package index
    secret: true                             # optional, default false
---
Key Required What it does title yes The runbook's name, shown when it runs. description no What the runbook is for. For people reading it; paulrun doesn't show it. output_path no Where to keep a transcript of each run. python no The command that runs Python blocks. inputs no Values paulrun asks for before it starts. See Inputs.

Every value must be text, except inputs, which is a list. Any other key is reported by check as a warning, so a typo like ouput_path doesn't go unnoticed, but it doesn't stop the runbook.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Inputs are values a runbook needs each time it runs, such as the version being released.

Key Required What it does name yes The input's name, in UPPER_SNAKE_CASE, e.g. VERSION or PUBLISH_TOKEN. description yes What to enter. Shown when paulrun asks for it. pattern no A regular expression the whole value must match, e.g. '^\d+\.\d+\.\d+$'. secret no true for passwords and tokens. See Secrets.

Each name can only be declared once, in the frontmatter or an input block. Other keys on an input are check warnings.

docs.title: How inputs are collected
docs.text:
Frontmatter inputs are all collected before the first step runs, in the order they're declared. Input blocks are collected the same way, but later, when the run reaches them.

  1. If an environment variable with the input's name is set, paulrun uses it without asking. VERSION=1.2.0 paulrun go RELEASING.md releases 1.2.0 with no prompt. An empty variable counts as not set.
  2. Otherwise paulrun asks for it, showing its name and description.

If the input has a pattern, the value must match all of it. A typed answer that doesn't match is refused and asked for again. A value from the environment that doesn't match stops paulrun with an error, before anything runs.

docs.title: Using inputs
docs.text:
Every input is set as an environment variable in every run block, so a shell block can read $VERSION and a Python block os.environ["VERSION"].

An input that isn't secret can also be written as a placeholder, <VERSION>, and paulrun replaces it with the value. Placeholders are replaced in:

  • run blocks, before they run
  • docstring and confirm blocks, before they're shown
  • output_path

Placeholders are never replaced in the rest of the runbook, so headings and prose are shown exactly as written. A placeholder is <, a capital letter, then capital letters, digits or underscores, then >. Anything else in angle brackets, such as <html>, is left alone.

Using a placeholder that isn't a declared input is a check error, as is declaring an input that nothing uses (a warning). Using an input as $VERSION in a run block counts as using it.

Placeholders are replaced as plain text

A value is put into a block exactly as entered. If someone enters 1.2.0; rm -rf ~ for <VERSION>, that's what the block runs. Give inputs that end up in commands a pattern, so only the values you expect get through.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
An input with secret: true is for something that mustn't be shown or saved, like an API token:

  • Its prompt hides what's typed.
  • It's never replaced as a placeholder. Read it from the environment instead, as $PUBLISH_TOKEN. Writing <PUBLISH_TOKEN> is a check error.
  • Its value is replaced with **** everywhere paulrun shows or records it: block output, the transcript, and anywhere it appears in the runbook itself.
  • paulrun go --dry doesn't ask for it at all.
uv publish --token "$PUBLISH_TOKEN"

What masking can't catch

paulrun hides a secret by spotting its exact value, one line at a time. A command that changes the value before printing it, for example by encoding it, or splits it across two lines, can still reveal it. Pass secrets to commands, rather than printing them.

docs.title: Input blocks
docs.text:
Some values don't exist until part way through a run: the number GitHub gives a pull request you've just opened, or a one-time code from an authenticator app that expires in seconds. An input block asks for one when the run reaches it, rather than before the first step:

## Open the pull request

```confirm
Open a pull request for <VERSION> on GitHub.
```

```input
name: PR
description: The number GitHub gave the pull request
pattern: '^\d+$'
```

```sh run
gh pr merge <PR>
```

An input block takes the same keys as a frontmatter input, written as YAML. It's collected the same way, from the environment if it's set or by asking, with its pattern checked. From then on it's like any other input: set in the environment of every later run block, filled in as a placeholder in later blocks if it isn't secret, and shown as **** if it is.

It pairs well with confirm: do this by hand, then tell paulrun what you got.

Since its value doesn't exist until the run reaches it:

  • Using it before the block, as <PR> or $PR, is a check error, and so is using it in output_path.
  • paulrun go --dry doesn't ask for it. It shows where the run would stop to ask, and later blocks show <PR> as written.
  • paulrun inputs lists it with the step that asks for it.

The text inside an input block is only read as YAML, so a placeholder in its description is just text.

An OTP is a good example of an input block that should be secret:

```input
name: OTP
description: The code from your authenticator app
pattern: '^\d{6}$'
secret: true
```

```sh run
npm publish --otp "$OTP"
```

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
Each ## heading starts a step, and its text is the step's name. A step holds every block until the next ## heading. ### and smaller headings are just text inside the current step.

A run, docstring, confirm or input block before the first ## heading doesn't belong to a step. That's a check error, so it can't be skipped without anyone noticing.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
A fenced code block's first line decides what paulrun does with it. The first word is the language, and a second word of run makes it a block paulrun runs.

Fence What paulrun does ```docstring Shows the text as it reaches it. ```confirm Shows the text, then waits for you to answer y. Any other answer ends the run. ```input Asks for an input when the run reaches it. See Input blocks. ```sh run Runs the block. See Run blocks. Any other fence, e.g. ```sh or ```python Nothing. It's documentation.

A plain ```sh fence is never run, so you can show a command without paulrun running it.

docs.title: docstring
docs.text:
Notes to show while the runbook runs, such as what's about to happen:

```docstring
Releasing <VERSION>. This takes a few minutes.
```

docs.title: confirm
docs.text:
A step only a person can do, like clicking a button on a website. paulrun shows the text and waits:

```confirm
Create a GitHub release from tag <VERSION>, then come back here.
```

Answer y to carry on. Any other answer, including just pressing enter, ends the run as aborted, and nothing after it runs.

docs.title: Run blocks
docs.text:
A block marked run is run by the backend for its language. Each block's output is shown as it's printed, and its exit code decides what happens next: 0 carries on, and anything else stops the run there.

Every block runs:

  • in the folder the runbook is in, wherever you run paulrun from
  • with paulrun's environment, plus every input
  • with PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1, so Python output isn't held back, and PAGER=cat and GIT_PAGER=cat, so nothing waits in a pager

Run paulrun backends to see which languages you can use. Other languages can be added with backends.

docs.title: Shell blocks
docs.text:
Languages: sh, bash, shell.

Each block runs as one bash script, so a variable set on one line is still set on the next. It stops at the first command that fails, including one early in a pipe, as if it began with set -eo pipefail.

check finds syntax errors with bash -n, and also uses shellcheck for warnings if it's installed.

docs.title: Python blocks
docs.text:
Languages: python, py.

Each block runs as its own script, so nothing is shared between blocks except the environment. By default it runs with the Python that paulrun runs on, so only the standard library is available. To use another interpreter, or your project's dependencies, set python in the frontmatter:

python: uv run python

python is any command; the block's script is added to the end of it. check reports an error if its first word isn't installed.

check finds syntax errors by compiling each block with paulrun's own Python, so syntax only a newer Python understands isn't caught.

docs.title: Blocks that ask for input
docs.text:
Blocks should run without anyone answering questions. A block can still ask on the terminal when it has to, the way git, ssh and gpg ask for a password, and that works normally. But anything it prints is shown line by line, so a question without a newline at the end isn't shown until you've answered it.

Values the runbook needs every time are better as inputs, and passwords and tokens as secrets.

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
Set output_path, and paulrun records each run in a plain text file:

output_path: logs/release-<VERSION>.md

The path is relative to the runbook, can use placeholders, and missing folders are created. Each run is added to the end of the file, so a failed attempt and the rerun that fixed it are both kept. A run that's never started, or a --dry run, isn't recorded.

--- paulrun RELEASING.md @ 2026-10-12T15:11:27+01:00
--- inputs: VERSION=1.2.0 PUBLISH_TOKEN=****

=== Run the tests ===
    make test
<everything make test printed>
exit 0 (4.2s)

=== Publish on GitHub ===
confirm: Create a GitHub release from tag 1.2.0. -> yes

=== Publish to PyPI ===
input: OTP=****
    uv publish --token "$PUBLISH_TOKEN"
skipped (--step)

--- finished: ok (3m12s)

Each run starts with a header and the inputs, with secrets as ****. Each step has its name, then each block's code, indented four spaces, followed by what it printed and its exit code and time. A confirm records its first line and the answer, an input block records its value where it was given (**** for a secret), and a block skipped with --step is marked as skipped. docstring blocks aren't recorded.

The last line says how the run ended:

Last line When --- finished: ok (3m12s) Every step ran. --- finished: failed at "<step>" (exit N) A block in that step exited with N. --- finished: aborted at "<step>" A confirm wasn't answered y, or you quit with --step. --- finished: interrupted at "<step>" You pressed Ctrl-C. A block that was running gets its exit line first.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• bash on macOS is version 3.2, and check can't find an unclosed heredoc (cat <<EOF with no EOF) with it. Newer versions of bash can.
  • Windows isn't supported.
